new.title: Explore Fort Rammekens near Vlissingen
new.desc: Built in 1547 at the mouth of the Westerschelde, this squat fort near Ritthem is called the oldest coastal fortification in Western Europe. Damp casemates, grassy ramparts and wide views over passing ships.
new.tip: It only opens on weekends from April to October, because bats hibernate inside in winter. Book ahead to be sure of getting in.

new.title: Step inside the caissons of the Watersnoodmuseum in Ouwerkerk
new.desc: The museum about the 1953 flood fills four giant concrete caissons that were sunk to close the last dike breach. Personal stories, models and hands-on displays explain why Zeeland lives behind the Delta Works.
new.tip: Walk up onto the dike behind the caissons afterwards: the creek left by the breach is still there.

new.title: Climb the church-tower lighthouse in Westkapelle
new.desc: 't Hoge Licht began life as a church tower; the church burned in 1831 and the tower became a lighthouse that still shines every night. From the top you see how low Westkapelle sits behind its sea dike.
new.tip: Tickets go via the Polderhuis dike and war museum on the same street; combine both and walk to the tank on the dike.

new.title: Look up at the unfinished Dikke Toren of Zierikzee
new.desc: Zierikzee's 62 metre Sint-Lievensmonstertoren was meant to be far taller, but the money ran out in the 1400s. Below it, the Oude Haven with its old ships and the Zuidhavenpoort gate make one of Zeeland's prettiest harbour scenes.
new.tip: Park at the edge of the old town; the centre is for residents. Shops are mostly shut on Sundays.

new.title: Spot the leaning tower of the Oude Kerk in Delft
new.desc: Delft's oldest church leans visibly over the Oude Delft canal, and its builders even bent the top back to compensate. Vermeer and the admirals Piet Hein and Maerten Tromp are buried inside.
new.tip: One ticket covers both the Oude and Nieuwe Kerk. It is closed on Sundays.

new.title: Read the stained-glass stories of the Sint-Janskerk in Gouda
new.desc: The Goudse Glazen hold about half of the Netherlands' surviving 16th-century stained glass, with Catholic and Protestant windows side by side in the country's longest church.
new.tip: Grab the free leaflet that explains each scene, then cross to the Museum Gouda garden to see full-size window designs.

new.title: Climb 275 steps up the Grote Kerk tower in Dordrecht
new.desc: The tower was planned at over 100 metres but stopped at 65 for fear it would collapse; in 1626 it got four colossal clock faces instead. From the top you see the rivers meeting and the Biesbosch beyond.
new.tip: The tower is open from April to October. On a very clear day you can pick out the tower of Breda.

new.title: Visit the steam tug Furie in Maassluis harbour
new.desc: Maassluis was the home port of the Dutch ocean towing fleet. The 1916 steam tug Furie, which spent sixty years in Sweden before coming home, has been a museum ship here since 1978.
new.tip: Combine it with the towing museum on the Hoogstraat. Maassluis is the last stop before Hoek van Holland on metro line B.

new.title: Look into Jan Blanken's dry dock in Hellevoetsluis
new.desc: Inside the star-shaped fortress of Hellevoetsluis lies a stone dry dock built between 1798 and 1822 for the navy, one of a kind in the Netherlands. A visitor centre and tours reveal the aqueducts that drained it.
new.tip: The old pump house is now a restaurant; walk the ramparts afterwards to the lighthouse at the harbour mouth.

new.title: See the lonely church tower of Goedereede
new.desc: Tiny Goedereede was once a busy port and its 1512 church was pulled down, but the tower survived and guided ships as a lighthouse until 1911. The future Pope Adrian VI was once parish priest here.
new.tip: Stroll the little harbour, then continue to the beach at Ouddorp, ten minutes away.

new.title: Slurp oysters beside the oyster pits of Yerseke
new.desc: Yerseke is Zeeland's shellfish village, and at the family-run Oesterij on the Havendijk you eat oysters right beside the 19th-century pits where they rest before sale.
new.tip: Ask for a tour of the oyster beds first, then taste the round Zeeuwse bolle against the long Zeeuwse creuse.

new.title: Eat a pan of mussels in Philippine
new.desc: This Zeeuws-Vlaanderen village lost its mussel harbour long ago but kept the restaurants, which serve around half a million kilos a year. Auberge des Moules has cooked them to the same family recipe for decades.
new.tip: Season runs roughly July to April. Use your first empty shell as tongs, like the locals do.

new.title: Try a sticky Zeeuwse bolus in Middelburg
new.desc: The spiral bun glazed in dark syrup and cinnamon is Zeeland's signature pastry. Bliek's version has been crowned the province's best bolus several times.
new.tip: Eat it warm with a coffee on the Markt in front of the Gothic town hall.

new.title: Buy boterbabbelaars at Diesch in Middelburg
new.desc: Zeeuwse babbelaars are hard butter candies, and JB Diesch has been boiling them in Middelburg since 1892. A tin makes the most Zeeland souvenir there is.
new.tip: The shop is on the Lange Noordstraat, a short walk from the Abdij and the Zeeuws Museum.

new.title: Spicy kibbeling at Foppe in Vlissingen
new.desc: A no-frills snack bar on the Bellamypark that seasons its fried fish chunks with Asian spices, a nod to Vlissingen's seafaring past.
new.tip: Take it up to the boulevard and eat while the ships pass.

new.title: Local oysters and fish at De Beuze in Zierikzee
new.desc: A seafood restaurant where Zierikzee locals go for Oosterschelde oysters and fresh fish, without the touristy prices of the harbour terraces.
new.tip: Book even on a quiet weekend; the town fills up fast.

new.title: Apple pie at Kobus Kuch on the Beestenmarkt in Delft
new.desc: Delft's favourite slice of appeltaart with whipped cream, served on a leafy square full of terraces.
new.tip: Whole pies can be ordered to take home.

new.title: Go inside the Delta Works at Neeltje Jans
new.desc: Deltapark Neeltje Jans sits on the artificial island in the middle of the Oosterscheldekering. See the storm barrier up close, relive the 1953 flood in the Delta Experience and take a boat onto the Oosterschelde to look for seals and porpoises.
new.tip: The park is seasonal, roughly spring to autumn; arrive early, as some tours stop later in the day.

new.title: Ride the steam train from Goes to Hoedekenskerke
new.desc: A heritage line puffs through the orchards and polders of Zuid-Beveland to the Westerschelde dike at Hoedekenskerke.
new.tip: On steam days the train only stops at Goes, Kwadendamme and Hoedekenskerke; check the running days in advance.

new.title: Walk into the Drowned Land of Saeftinghe
new.desc: Europe's largest brackish salt marsh covers villages swallowed by the Westerschelde. Creeks fill and empty with tides of up to six metres, and harriers and bearded tits hunt over the reeds.
new.tip: Two short trails from the visitor centre are open to everyone; the heart of the marsh is only accessible on a guided excursion.
new.q: Bezoekerscentrum Verdronken Land van Saeftinghe, Emmaweg 4, Nieuw-Namen

new.title: Watch giant ships from the boulevard in Vlissingen
new.desc: Ships heading for Antwerp pass the Boulevard de Ruyter perhaps closer than anywhere else in the world. Admiral Michiel de Ruyter, born here, watches from his statue.
new.tip: Find the Belgian pilots' houses on the Spuistraat, where pilots still board the ships.

new.title: Watch the kitesurfers at the Brouwersdam
new.desc: The dam between Goeree-Overflakkee and Schouwen is a magnet for kitesurfers, windsurfers and sailors, with the North Sea on one side and the calm Grevelingen on the other.
new.tip: Stay for sunset at one of the beach pavilions on the sea side.

new.title: Paint a tile at Royal Delft
new.desc: De Porceleyne Fles is the last 17th-century factory still making Delft Blue by hand. Watch the master painters at work, then try the brush yourself in a tile-painting workshop.
new.tip: Book the workshop ahead, and leave time for the museum's tulip pyramids.

new.title: See Gouda by Candlelight
new.desc: On the second Friday of December, Gouda switches off its street lights and the houses around the Markt glow with candles. The highlight is lighting the Christmas tree sent every year by Norwegian sister city Kongsberg.
new.tip: Be on the Markt before eight in the evening for the countdown; walk in from the station to skip traffic.

new.title: Ferry to the wild island of Tiengemeten
new.desc: This former farming island in the Haringvliet was handed back to nature: about 700 hectares of wetland where you can wander freely. There is a Rien Poortvliet museum and a farmhouse inn.
new.tip: The year-round ferry leaves from Nieuwendijk near Zuid-Beijerland in the Hoeksche Waard; in summer boats also run from Hellevoetsluis.
